summary: This standards-track RFC defines Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, a simplified way to use BFD with most negotiation removed. That brings quick provisioning and better control and flexibility for nodes starting path monitoring. It updates RFC 5880.

eli5.summary: Quickly checking whether a path is alive without the usual back-and-forth setup.

questions: how does s-bfd differ from bfd
subtitle: A stripped-down BFD where a node can test a remote target instantly, with no session setup handshake.

tldr.problem: Classical BFD needs the two ends to negotiate a session and walk through state changes before a continuity test can start, which delays testing and means both ends must hold active session state.
tldr.mechanism: Each node allocates an S-BFD Discriminator for its local entities and runs a Reflector session that simply answers packets carrying that value. Any node that knows the value can send a Control packet and get an immediate reply.
tldr.outcome: The initiator can test a path as soon as it wants to, and the responder keeps no per-initiator state. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5880.

today: RFC 7880 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2016 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 5880, and the data-plane details for IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS are in RFC 7881.

sections.title: Why Seamless BFD
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880) is a general way to detect failures between two forwarding points. Seamless BFD (S-BFD) is a simplified use of BFD in which a large proportion of the negotiation is removed. The RFC lists quick provisioning and better control and flexibility for the nodes that start path monitoring as the benefits.

The key idea is removing the delay between a node wanting to run a continuity test and finishing it. In classical BFD terms, the initial change from DOWN to UP is virtually nonexistent. That removed delay is the "seam", which is where the name comes from. S-BFD reuses existing BFD implementations and machinery, and gives a largely stateless infrastructure for continuity testing.
sections.eli5: Usually you wait for a slow hello-and-reply routine before you can check a connection. S-BFD skips the waiting so the check happens right away.

sections.title: Terms and the Cast of Characters
sections.content:
S-BFD adds a small vocabulary on top of BFD. An entity is a function on a node that remote nodes may test, such as plain reachability, an IP address, a Router-ID or some other function.

  • SBFDInitiator: a session on a node that tests a remote entity by sending S-BFD packets. The node hosting it is the Initiator.
  • SBFDReflector: a session that listens for S-BFD Control packets aimed at local entities and generates responses. The node hosting it is the Responder. It is also called a Reflector BFD session.
  • S-BFD Discriminator: a BFD Discriminator allocated for a local entity. A plain BFD Discriminator is one allocated for an SBFDInitiator.

An S-BFD packet is either an S-BFD Control packet or an S-BFD Echo packet. The reader is expected to know BFD, IP and MPLS terms.
sections.eli5: One side is the asker and the other is the answerer. The answerer has a special name tag for each thing that can be checked, and it answers anyone who calls that name.

sections.title: How a Test Works
sections.content:
An S-BFD module on each node allocates one or more S-BFD Discriminators for its local entities and creates a Reflector BFD session. Applications such as OSPF or IS-IS may advertise the discriminators, so other nodes learn which value belongs to which remote entity.

Once that is in place, any node that knows a remote entity's discriminator can test it by sending S-BFD Control packets with that value in the Your Discriminator field. In the RFC's IS-IS example, node A allocates discriminator 123 and node D allocates 456, and each advertises its value in an IS-IS TLV. When A wants to check D, it sends a Control packet with Your Discriminator set to 456. D's Reflector session replies, which completes the test for A.

If a node allocates several S-BFD Discriminators, how remote nodes work out which one belongs to which entity is unspecified. The RFC therefore discourages using multiple S-BFD Discriminators on one node until a mapping method is defined.
sections.eli5: If you know a friend's secret knock, you can knock and get an answer straight away. Nobody has to agree on anything first.

sections.title: The Reflector Session and Discriminators
sections.content:
An S-BFD Discriminator MUST be unique within an administrative domain. If two nodes used the same value, a packet could end up at the wrong node and still get a reply because the Your Discriminator matches.

To reduce collisions, an SBFDInitiator takes its discriminator from the BFD Discriminator pool, which SHOULD be shared with classical BFD sessions on the same system. An SBFDReflector takes its value from an S-BFD Discriminator pool, which SHOULD be separate. Reflector values may be derived from things such as a System-ID, Router-ID or IP address, so a separate pool avoids clashing with other sessions.

A Reflector BFD session has three firm characteristics:

  • It MUST NOT send any S-BFD packet because a local timer expired.
  • It MUST answer a received S-BFD Control packet that carries a valid S-BFD Discriminator, unless local policy (administrative, security, rate limiter) forbids it.
  • It MUST be able to send only two states: UP and AdminDown.

One Reflector session may handle all local discriminators, or several may each handle a subset. That is a local matter.
sections.eli5: The answerer never speaks first. It only replies when someone calls out one of its names, and every name must belong to just one answerer.

sections.title: Initiator and Responder Procedures
sections.content:
S-BFD packets are demultiplexed using lower-layer information, for example a dedicated UDP port (RFC 7881) or an associated channel type (RFC 7885). The responder discards a packet whose Your Discriminator is not one of its local entries. If local policy allows, the matching Reflector session answers.

The Reflector builds its reply per RFC 5880, with these differences: State is UP or AdminDown only, Demand is 0, and My Discriminator and Your Discriminator are swapped from the received packet. Detect Mult and Desired Min TX Interval are copied. Required Min RX Interval tells initiators how fast they may send, so the Reflector can slow them down based on its load. The state is UP if the monitored entity is in service and SHOULD be AdminDown if it is temporarily out of service.

An SBFDInitiator always sets Demand to 1, sets Your Discriminator to the remote entity's value, and sets both Required Min RX Interval and Required Min Echo RX Interval to 0. It needs its own locally unique My Discriminator. The remote value may be learnt from routing protocols or configured locally.

If the initiator gets an AdminDown reply, it MUST NOT conclude reachability is lost and MUST back off its sending to no faster than 1 second. If enough packets fail to arrive, it SHOULD declare loss of reachability. For the very first packet it must allow for the latency to the responder and back.
sections.eli5: The answerer just flips the note around and sends it back, and says "I'm here" or "I'm taking a break". If it is busy, it can ask the asker to knock less often.

sections.title: The Initiator State Machine
sections.content:
An SBFDInitiator can be a persistent session with a timer (stateful), or a script or tool that sends packets only when needed (stateless). The classical BFD state machine does not work for stateful initiators because the Reflector never sends the INIT state.

The RFC therefore recommends a two-state machine: DOWN and UP. A received UP moves the initiator from DOWN to UP, which is the key difference from RFC 5880. A received AdminDown or a Detection Timer expiry moves it back to DOWN.

The Poll Sequence can be used in both directions and works as in RFC 5880. A Reflector may set the Poll bit to slow the initiator, and the initiator then answers with the Final bit set. A Reflector that receives a packet with the Poll bit set MUST respond with Poll cleared and Final set.
sections.eli5: The asker only has two moods: "it's alive" and "it's not". One good answer makes it happy, and silence or a "taking a break" note makes it worried.

sections.title: Echo, Loops and Security
sections.content:
The S-BFD Echo function sends packets addressed to the sender itself that U-turn on the target in the data plane. They MUST NOT be processed by any Reflector session. The RFC recommends always sending Control packets together with Echo packets. Control packets confirm the target is really reachable and can reveal when it goes out of service. Echo packets can be spoofed and can U-turn at a transit node, so some form of authentication MAY still be used.

Security considerations from RFC 5880 apply. Reflectors stay stateless, so a Reflector MUST NOT use the crypto sequence number to decide whether to accept a packet. It MUST accept a packet if authentication succeeds and MUST reuse the received sequence number in its reply. The initiator accepts only a sequence number in the permissible range. The RFC strongly encourages strong authentication, because Simple Password authentication can put other services at risk if the password is reused.

Appendix A describes a reflection loop. A man in the middle could spoof a packet between two S-BFD nodes so that each reflects it to the other forever, since reflected packets have TTL 255. The fix is the Demand bit: initiators always set it and Reflectors always clear it. A Reflector discards a packet with D cleared, and an initiator discards a packet with D set.

Operationally, deployments SHOULD stop persistent S-BFD packets from leaking outside the administrative domain. Across multiple hops a congestion control mechanism MUST be implemented.
sections.eli5: If two answerers kept bouncing one note back and forth, it would never end. So every note is marked as "question" or "answer", and answers are never bounced again.
